FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]

            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)

INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

═══════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Underfill), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, NCR, SOP
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- DemoBottling-Shift-Log-2026-09-10-Night.csv (underfill alarm details) – TIER 2 EVENT – HIGH confidence
- FL‑101‑SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – TIER 2 DOCUMENT – HIGH confidence
- FL‑101‑NCR.txt (NCR‑2026‑012) – TIER 2 DOCUMENT – HIGH confidence
- WI‑FL101‑001 (Work Instruction) – TIER 2 DOCUMENT – HIGH confidence
- Knowledge‑graph entry for FL‑101 (underfill fault, systemic rule, seal‑kit part data) – TIER 1 VERIFIED – HIGH confidence

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: worn fill‑valve seals on valves 9, 15 and 3 causing drip between fills, triggering three underfill alarms in one shift (systemic fault) – evidence from alarm log (dripping valves) and SOP/knowledge‑graph seal‑wear criteria.
- Difference vs historical pattern: first recorded underfill alarms on Filling Line 1; previous NCR‑2026‑012 involved different valves (7, 12, 13, 19) but the same failure mode (worn seals). No prior underfill events in earlier shift logs.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped for seal‑replacement; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour including sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check.
- Safety risk: LOW (no injury reported) – but LOTO required per SOP.
- Financial impact: downtime cost plus potential reject loss; exact monetary value not provided.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH – three underfill alarms in one shift meet the “systemic fault” rule; production stop and LOTO are required.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety – Press STOP, apply LOTO (SAF‑003) and isolate power before any work.
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Inspect valves 9, 15, 3 for dripping; confirm underfill source via checkweigher report.
  Step 3: Fix – Replace the fill‑valve seals on the identified valves using WI‑FL101‑001:
    1. Drain bowl below valve level.
    2. Remove each valve with valve key (quarter turn left).
    3. Remove old seal and O‑ring, clean seat.
    4. Install new SEAL‑FV‑24 kit seal and O‑ring, apply food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1.
    5. Re‑fit valve (quarter turn right) and secure.
    6. Remove LOTO, refill bowl.
    7. Perform mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min clean water).
  Step 4: Verify – Run first‑bottle check: weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml. If any out of range, stop and re‑inspect valve.
  Step 5: Quality – Quarantine any bottles produced during the alarm period; record results in maintenance log and sign‑off by shift supervisor.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Replace worn seals on valves 9, 15, 3 and adjust maintenance interval to ensure seal replacement every 3 months or 1 500 running hours, whichever comes first.

- Preventive action:
  - Add valve‑drip inspection to the hourly checkweigher review.

12.4 Product Supply Pressure Low
Alarm message: "Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar"

Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill.

Causes, most common first:
  1. Supply filter blocked — clean or replace the filter (FLT-PS-10)
  2. Air in the supply line — bleed the air using the bleed valve on the bowl
  3. Supply tank running low — check the tank level with the water
     treatment room

  Step 2 — Clean the supply filter.
  Step 3 — Bleed air from the supply line.
  Step 4 — Confirm the pressure is back to 1.5 to 2.0 bar.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]

            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)

INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

═══════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Underfill), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, SOP, NCR
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- DemoBottling-Shift-Log-2026-09-10-Night.csv – underfill alarm timestamps (3 occurrences) – TIER 2 – HIGH confidence
- FL-101-SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – sections 11, 12.1, 12.4, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4 – TIER 2 – HIGH confidence
- FL-101-NCR.txt – NCR‑2026‑012 details of prior seal replacements – TIER 2 – HIGH confidence
- WI-FL101-001 (Work Instruction) – seal‑kit replacement steps – TIER 2 – HIGH confidence
- Knowledge Graph (verified) – fault definition, systemic rule, correct response, specifications – TIER 1 – VERIFIED

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Dripping fill‑valve seals on valves 9, 15 and 3 caused under‑fill alarms; three alarms in one shift trigger the systemic fault rule. (Evidence: alarm log showing dripping valves, SOP/knowledge‑graph stating “worn fill valve seal” as primary cause, and systemic rule for ≥3 alarms.)
- Difference from historical pattern: First recorded under‑fill alarms on Filling Line 1; previous NCR‑2026‑012 addressed seals on other valves but no recent alarms were logged.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line stopped for seal‑kit replacement and required sanitation rinse; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO and PPE; production stop qualifies as high‑risk fault).
- Financial impact: Approximate loss of one hour of production plus labor for maintenance; exact cost not quantified in provided data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH – three under‑fill alarms in a single shift meet the “systemic fault” threshold; safety procedures (LOTO) are required and production is stopped.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action
  Step 1: Safety – Press STOP, apply LOTO per SAF‑003, wear safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, and hearing protection.
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Inspect fill valves 9, 15 and 3 for dripping; confirm seal wear; verify product‑supply pressure is within 1.5–2.0 bar.
  Step 3: Fix – Replace the worn seal kits on the identified valves using the approved procedure:
    1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO).
    2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level.
    3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left).
    4. Remove the old seal and O‑ring with the seal pick.
    5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint‑free cloth and check it for scratches.
    6. Fit the new seal and O‑ring from the SEAL‑FV‑24 kit with a thin layer of food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1.
    7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks).
    8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl.
    9. Perform the mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min clean water rinse of bowl, valves and nozzles).
    10. Conduct the mandatory first‑bottle check: run at normal speed, weigh the first 20 bottles; all must be 495–505 ml. Shift supervisor signs off.
  Step 4: Verify – Confirm product‑supply pressure is 1.5–2.0 bar, no further dripping, and that the first‑bottle check passed. Record results in the maintenance log.
  Step 5: Quality – Quarantine any bottles rejected by the checkweigher during the fault; re‑weigh and disposition per quality protocol.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution)
  • Replace all worn fill‑valve seals on the line and adjust the preventive‑maintenance interval to every 3 months or 1 500 running hours, whichever comes first.
  • Update the seal‑wear monitoring log and ensure the checkweigher reject count is reviewed hourly.

- Preventive action
  • Implement a daily pre‑shift check of fill‑valve seals for dripping.
  • Add an alarm‑trend review: if two under‑fill alarms occur before shift end, raise a maintenance work order immediately.
  • Reinforce the “Do NOT increase fill time to fix under‑fill” rule in shift briefings.

1. PURPOSE

This work instruction explains how to replace the seal kit in an FL-101
fill valve. A worn seal is the most common cause of underfill alarms.

2. SCOPE

3. WHEN TO REPLACE THE SEALS

---

[Source: FL-101-Work-Instruction.txt | Type: Work Instruction | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.86]
2. SCOPE

Applies to all 24 fill valves on the FL-101 Bottle Filler. Only trained
maintenance technicians may carry out this work.

3. WHEN TO REPLACE THE SEALS

Replace the seal kit when:
  - A valve drips between fills
  - The checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again
  - Three or more underfill alarms happen in one shift
  - The seal has reached its limit: 3 months or 1,500 running hours,
    whichever comes first

4. TIME NEEDED

  One valve:                     about 15 minutes
  A typical job (1 to 4 valves): 30 to 45 minutes
  Including rinse and check:     about 1 hour

5. PARTS AND TOOLS

  Seal kit, one per valve:  SEAL-FV-24 (main seal and O-ring)
  Food-grade lubricant:     FGL-1
  Location:                 Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
  Tools:                    valve key, seal pick, clean lint-free cloths,
                            20 empty 500 ml bottles for the check

6. SAFETY

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]
      correct response: Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor

══════════════════════════════════════════════════

═══════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Underfill), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, NCR, SOP
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:

- FL‑101‑NCR.txt – NCR‑2026‑012 (underfill alarms, corrective actions completed)
- FL‑101‑SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – sections 11, 12.1, 12.4, 6.2, 6.1, 6.3, 6.4, 8.1, 10, 13
- FL‑101‑Work‑Instruction.txt (WI‑FL101‑001 Rev 1.0) – seal‑kit replacement procedure
- Knowledge‑graph entries (verified) – fault definition, systemic rule, specifications, safety requirements

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: worn fill‑valve seals on valves 9, 15 and 3 causing dripping and underfill alarms (evidence from alarm log, SOP “worn seal” cause, and past NCR indicating seal wear as primary failure mode)
- Difference vs history: previous NCR‑2026‑012 addressed seals on valves 7, 12, 13, 19; current alarms involve different valves, indicating a new set of seals have reached wear limit despite no recorded recent service

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line must be stopped for seal replacement; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour including sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check
- Safety risk: LOW (no injury or hazardous material reported; safety steps are standard LOTO and PPE)
- Financial impact: downtime cost proportional to 1 hour of line loss plus labor for seal change (exact dollar amount not provided)

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms in a single shift trigger the “systemic underfill” rule in the SOP, requiring immediate production stop and maintenance action

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Press STOP, apply LOTO (SAF‑003), wear safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, and hearing protection
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Retrieve the checkweigher report, identify under‑filling valves (9, 15, 3), inspect each for dripping seal
  Step 3: Fix — Replace seal kits on valves 9, 15, 3 following WI‑FL101‑001 steps:
    1. Drain bowl below valve level
    2. Remove valve with valve key
    3. Remove old seal and O‑ring
    4. Clean seat, inspect for scratches
    5. Install new SEAL‑FV‑24 kit with food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1
    6. Refit valve, remove lock, refill bowl
    7. Perform mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min)
  Step 4: Verify — Run first‑bottle check: weigh first 20 bottles, all must be 495‑505 ml; confirm product supply pressure 1.5‑2.0 bar; record results and have shift supervisor sign off
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced during the fault, log seal‑kit part numbers, hours on seal, and operator name in maintenance log; update NCR record if recurrence occurs
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Replace all worn seals, ensure fill‑time remains at factory setting 3.2 s, and adjust maintenance interval if wear is occurring faster than 3 months/1 500 h
- Preventive action: 
  • Add hourly checkweigher reject monitoring and trigger work order at first sign of underfill
  • Reinforce SOP training: operators must NOT change fill time to compensate for underfill
  • Schedule seal inspections every 3 months or 1 500 h and track wear trends
  • Review spare‑part stock levels to ensure kits are available
- Who to notify: Maintenance supervisor, Shift lead, Quality lead, Production control

═══════════════════════════════════════
PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

SITUATION: Three underfill alarms occurred on FL‑101 during the night shift, indicating worn fill‑valve seals.
ROOT CAUSE: Seals on valves 9, 15 and 3 have worn past their service interval, causing dripping and underfill.
STATUS: Line stopped for seal replacement; expected to restart after ~1 hour of work and verification.
ACTION REQUIRED: Apply LOTO, replace the three seal kits per WI‑FL101‑001, perform sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check before restarting.
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued underfill will trigger further alarms, force an unscheduled shutdown, and may lead to product non‑conformance or larger production loss.

ALARM PATTERN FINDINGS:
- Frequency: 3 underfill alarms recorded in the 2026‑09‑10 night shift log (all within the same shift).  
- Most recent prior event: No prior underfill alarm events are present in the available shift‑log data.  
- Pattern: The underfill alarm was triggered repeatedly during the night shift on FL‑101. Each alarm was preceded by reports of dripping valves (initially valves 9 and 15, later valve 3 added). The log notes the alarms but does not record any resolution actions or subsequent changes to the filling process.  
- What is different this time:  
  1. This is the first documented occurrence of an underfill alarm on FL‑101 in the provided data set.  
  2. The alarm sequence escalated from two valves (9 & 15) to a third valve (3), indicating a widening issue.  
  3. Multiple alarms in quick succession suggest a persistent problem rather than an isolated event.  
- Data confidence: HIGH

- Corrective actions completed: Replacement of worn seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19; implementation of SOP change to prohibit altering fill time; stocking of spare seal kits; inclusion of seal replacement interval in the maintenance schedule; verification that fill time returned to 3.2 s and underfill rate fell below 0.5 % over three weeks.

SOP / PROCEDURE FINDINGS:
- Correct response procedure:  
  1. **Alarm “Fill level low — bottles under target volume”**  
     - Identify cause (worn fill valve seal, blocked nozzle, low product supply pressure).  
     - If due to low product supply pressure:  
       1. Press STOP.  
       2. Clean the supply filter (FLT‑PS‑10).  
       3. Bleed air from the supply line using the bleed valve on the bowl.  
       4. Confirm pressure is back to **1.5–2.0 bar** (alarm threshold is 1.3 bar).  
       5. Restart machine.  
       6. Weigh the first 20 bottles; all must be **495–505 ml**.  
  2. **General underfill alarm**  
     - Check fill valve seal for dripping.  
     - Inspect fill nozzle for debris.  
     - Verify product supply pressure (see 12.4).  
- Key specifications:  
  - Product supply pressure alarm threshold: **< 1.3 bar**.  
  - Acceptable bottle volume: **495–505 ml**.  
  - Restart pressure requirement: **1.5–2.0 bar**.  
- Safety requirements:  
  - Press STOP before performing any maintenance.  
  - Use appropriate PPE when cleaning filters or bleeding air (gloves, eye protection).  
  - Ensure the machine is fully stopped and isolated before inspecting valves or nozzles.  
- SOP gap: **NO — procedure exists**  
- Data confidence: **HIGH**

SOURCES USED:
- FL‑101‑SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – sections 12.1, 12.4, 11. Checks During the Shift.
KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]
      correct response: Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor
      meaning: Several worn seals: a systemic fault, not bad luck
      trigger: 3 or more underfill alarms in one shift
      then required: Fill Valve Seal Replacement (details above)
      then required: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 13]
          electrical rule: Do not attempt electrical repairs. Always call maintenance.
          trigger 3: Any electrical fault code shows on the control panel
          trigger 4: A guide rail will not lock in position
          trigger 5: Any glass breakage (also call the quality lead)
          trigger 1: The same alarm happens 3 or more times in one shift
          trigger 2: Underfill continues after the seals have been replaced

Machine-wide safety (applies to any work on this machine):
  LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  PPE Required on Filling Line 1  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.1]
      feet: Safety shoes
      hands: Cut-resistant gloves when handling glass or change parts
      hearing: Hearing protection
      eyes: Safety glasses at all times
  Machine Safety Rules  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 6.3 and 6.4]
      air rule: Never use compressed air near open bottles or broken glass
      rule: Never clear a jam while the machine is running, never reach past a guard, and never bypass or tape over a guard switch
      floor: Keep the floor dry. Report leaks and spills straight away.
      guards: All guard doors have safety switches; the machine stops if a guard door is opened

Other faults this machine can have (not matching this incident): Overfill; Infeed Jam; Glass Breakage; Product Supply Pressure Low


Critical warnings:
  ⚠️  First-Bottle Check is MANDATORY — true — normal production must not restart without it  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
  ⚠️  LOTO (SAF-003): Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]

  ⚠️  For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
  ⚠️  Machine Safety Rules: Never clear a jam while the machine is running, never reach past a guard, and never bypass or tape over a guard switch  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 6.3 and 6.4]
  ⚠️  Do NOT: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  ⚠️  Do NOT: raise the fill time to fix underfill

1. PURPOSE

This work instruction explains how to replace the seal kit in an FL-101
fill valve. A worn seal is the most common cause of underfill alarms.

2. SCOPE

Applies to all 24 fill valves on the FL-101 Bottle Filler. Only trained
maintenance technicians may carry out this work.

3. WHEN TO REPLACE THE SEALS

2. SCOPE

Applies to all 24 fill valves on the FL-101 Bottle Filler. Only trained
maintenance technicians may carry out this work.

3. WHEN TO REPLACE THE SEALS

Replace the seal kit when:
  - A valve drips between fills
  - The checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again
  - Three or more underfill alarms happen in one shift
  - The seal has reached its limit: 3 months or 1,500 running hours,
    whichever comes first

4. TIME NEEDED

  One valve:                     about 15 minutes
  A typical job (1 to 4 valves): 30 to 45 minutes
  Including rinse and check:     about 1 hour

5. PARTS AND TOOLS

  Seal kit, one per valve:  SEAL-FV-24 (main seal and O-ring)
  Food-grade lubricant:     FGL-1
  Location:                 Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
  Tools:                    valve key, seal pick, clean lint-free cloths,
                            20 empty 500 ml bottles for the check

6. SAFETY

---

  - The shift supervisor must sign off the first-bottle check before normal
    production restarts.
  - Record in the maintenance log: date, valve numbers changed, seal kits

  What you see                        Check                     Action
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Valve still drips                   Seal seated correctly?    Refit the seal

  All valves underfill                Supply pressure?          SOP Section 12.4
  Overfill for 2 to 3 minutes only    Normal settling           No action
  Overfill after 5 minutes            Valve fully clicked in?   Refit the valve
  Leak at the valve body              O-ring missing?           Fit a new O-ring

1. WHAT HAPPENED
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

On the night shift of 16 January 2026, FL-101 raised underfill alarms
three times: at 21:40, 23:55 and 02:10.

After each alarm the operator increased the fill time to push more water
into the bottles: first from 3.2 to 3.6 seconds, then to 3.9 seconds.

The longer fill time made most valves overflow. Water spilled onto the
bottles and the conveyor, labels were damaged at the labeller, and the
line stopped twice to clean up spillage.

---

[Source: FL-101-NCR.txt | Type: NCR | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.84]

8. LESSONS LEARNED
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  - Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise. Check for dripping
    valves first.
  - Never increase the fill time to fix underfill. It hides worn seals and
    causes overflow.

12.4 Product Supply Pressure Low
Alarm message: "Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar"

Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill.

Causes, most common first:
  1. Supply filter blocked — clean or replace the filter (FLT-PS-10)
  2. Air in the supply line — bleed the air using the bleed valve on the bowl
  3. Supply tank running low — check the tank level with the water
     treatment room

  Step 1 — Press STOP.
  Step 2 — Clean the supply filter.
  Step 3 — Bleed air from the supply line.
  Step 4 — Confirm the pressure is back to 1.5 to 2.0 bar.
  Step 5 — Restart, then weigh the first 20 bottles. All must be 495 to 505 ml.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill

INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

═══════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Underfill), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, Maintenance, SOP, NCR
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑10‑Night.csv (2026‑09‑10) – underfill alarms for valves 9, 15, 3
- FL‑101‑SOP.txt Rev 1.0 (no timestamp) – alarm definition, response procedure, safety steps, specifications
- FL‑101‑Work‑Instruction.txt (no timestamp) – seal‑kit part number, replacement steps, interval
- FL‑101‑NCR.txt (2026‑01‑16) – prior seal‑replacement NCR‑2026‑012 and corrective actions
- Knowledge Graph for FL‑101 (verified) – consolidated facts on causes, systemic fault rule, mandatory steps
- WI‑FL101‑001 (work instruction referenced in knowledge graph) – detailed seal‑replacement procedure

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Worn fill‑valve seal kits on valves 9, 15 and 3 are dripping between fills, triggering underfill alarms.
- Difference vs. history: This shift recorded three underfill alarms (≥3 in one shift) and added a new valve 3, indicating a systemic fault rather than an isolated single‑valve event.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line must be stopped for seal replacement; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour including sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO, PPE, and mandatory safety steps before any work).
- Financial impact: Lost production for ~1 hour plus labor for seal change; exact cost not quantified in provided data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Justification: Three or more underfill alarms in a single shift meet the systemic fault rule (knowledge graph) and require immediate production stop and maintenance work order.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action (follow knowledge‑graph steps, safety first):
Step 1: Safety — Press STOP, apply LOTO per SAF‑003, wear safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, and hearing protection.
Step 2: Diagnosis — Review the checkweigher report; confirm dripping on valves 9, 15, 3; tag each valve with a green tag.
Step 3: Fix — Replace the seal kit (SEAL‑FV‑24) on each affected valve using WI‑FL101‑001:
  1. Drain bowl below valve level.
  2. Remove valve with valve key (quarter turn left).
  3. Remove old seal and O‑ring with seal pick.
  4. Clean seat; inspect for scratches (report if scratched).
  5. Install new seal and O‑ring, apply thin layer of food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1.
  6. Re‑install valve (quarter turn right until click).
  7. Count tools/parts, remove lock, refill bowl.
  8. Perform mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min clean water).
Step 4: Verify — Run first‑bottle check: weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495–505 ml. If any out of range, stop and re‑inspect.
Step 5: Quality — Record seal‑change details (valve numbers, old seal condition, kit used, technician name) in maintenance log; quarantine first‑bottle batch until verified.

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Replace all worn seals on the identified valves and any other valves approaching the 3‑month/1 500‑hour interval; ensure fill‑time remains at the factory‑set 3.2 s (do NOT adjust).

Preventive action:
- Add hourly checkweigher reject monitoring; if rejects > 1/100, notify shift lead immediately.
- Schedule seal‑kit replacement every 3 months or 1 500 hours, whichever comes first, and track wear signs (flattened, cracked, discoloured).
- Update maintenance work order system to generate alerts when three or more underfill alarms occur in a shift.
- Conduct a brief refresher on “Do NOT increase fill time to mask underfill” for all operators.

Who to notify:
- Shift lead (immediate alarm response)
- Maintenance supervisor (authorise seal‑change work order)
- Quality lead (record NCR follow‑up and first‑bottle verification)

═══════════════════════════════════════
PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

SOP / PROCEDURE FINDINGS:
- Correct response procedure:  
  1. **Identify the cause** – Check the alarm message.  
     - If “Fill level low — bottles under target volume” (Underfill):  
       a. Inspect fill valve seals for wear (look for dripping).  
       b. Inspect fill nozzles for debris.  
       c. Check product supply pressure.  
     - If “Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar”:  
       a. Press STOP.  
       b. Clean or replace the supply filter (FLT‑PS‑10).  
       c. Bleed air from the supply line using the bleed valve on the bowl.  
       d. Verify pressure is restored to 1.5–2.0 bar.  
       e. Restart the line.  
       f. Weigh the first 20 bottles; all must be 495–505 ml.  
  2. **During shift checks** – Every hour weigh 5 bottles (must be 495–505 ml) and record checkweigher rejects.  
  3. **If reject count >1/100** – Notify shift lead; rising rejects often indicate worn seals.  
  4. **If underfill persists after pressure correction** – Inspect fill valves for dripping and nozzles for blockage.  
- Key specifications:  
  - Product supply pressure target: **1.5–2.0 bar** (alarm if <1.3 bar).  
  - Bottle weight target: **495–505 ml**.  
  - Reject tolerance: **≤1 bottle per 100** during an hour.  
- Safety requirements:  
  - Press STOP before performing filter cleaning or bleeding.  
  - Use appropriate PPE when handling filters and bleed valves (gloves, eye protection).  
  - Ensure the line is fully stopped before inspecting valves or nozzles.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.

  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.

                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product

                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: worn fill‑valve seals causing dripping between fills, leading to underfill alarms (evidence from SOP, work instruction, NCR, and knowledge graph).
- Difference from historical pattern: current report does not mention valve drip, but three underfill alarms in one shift match the systemic fault pattern that indicates multiple worn seals; the lack of explicit valve observation is a deviation that must be investigated.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped or operating at reduced speed until underfill is corrected; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour including sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO and stop of production; underfill alarms trigger systemic fault rule).
- Financial impact: not quantified in supplied data; downtime and potential reject of out‑of‑spec bottles imply loss of product and labor.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms occurred in a single shift, meeting the systemic fault rule that mandates production stop and maintenance work order.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Press STOP, isolate power, apply LOTO (SAF‑003) and wear required PPE (safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, hearing protection).
  Step 2: Diagnosis — 
    - Retrieve the checkweigher report to identify which valve numbers are underfilling. 
    - Visually inspect those valves for dripping between fills. 
    - Verify product supply pressure is ≥ 1.3 bar; if low, follow low‑pressure procedure (clean filter FLT‑PS‑10, bleed line, confirm 1.5‑2.0 bar). 
    - If no drip and pressure is normal, inspect fill nozzle for blockage.
